questions.question: Why does Nepal's vegetation change from sal forest to rhododendron to alpine meadow as you climb?
questions.solution: Temperature falls ~6 °C per 1000 m and rainfall patterns shift — each altitude band offers a different climate envelope. Each dominant species (sal: warm lowland; rhododendron: cool mid-hills; alpine herbs: cold heights) is adapted to its band's temperature and moisture. Climate zonation drives vegetation zonation.

questions.question: What makes a species 'dominant' in a community, and why does losing a dominant hurt the whole community?
questions.solution: Dominance = greatest biomass/cover and greatest control over the community's conditions (a sal forest's canopy sets light, humidity and soil for everything beneath). Remove the dominant and the microclimate collapses — shade species, soil organisms and dependents lose their habitat. Dominants are ecosystem engineers.

questions.question: Describe the stages of succession on bare rock and explain what drives the progression from lichen to forest.
questions.solution: Lichens colonise bare rock, secreting acids that weather it into primitive soil → mosses deepen the soil → grasses and herbs → shrubs → trees. Each stage modifies the environment (more soil, more shade, more moisture) in ways that favour the NEXT stage more than itself — the community builds its own replacement. The endpoint is the climax community in equilibrium with the local climate.

questions.question: Why are lichens and mosses the pioneers on bare rock — what traits suit them for the harshest stage?
questions.solution: They need almost no soil (attach directly to rock), tolerate extreme drought and temperature, are tiny and slow-growing, and can survive on bare mineral surfaces and air-borne nutrients. Their job is to CREATE soil, which larger plants then need. Pioneers are stress-tolerant; later species are competitors.

questions.question: Why does overgrazing degrade grassland faster than an equal amount of mowing?
questions.solution: Grazing animals uproot and trample seedlings, compact the soil (reducing infiltration and root growth) and select out palatable species — the sward shifts to unpalatable, weedy plants. Mowing cuts biomass but leaves roots and soil structure intact. Repeated biomass removal + soil damage = regeneration failure.

questions.question: Climbing a mountain produces the same sequence of vegetation zones as travelling toward the poles. Why?
questions.solution: The underlying variable in both cases is temperature (and its effect on growing season and moisture): temperature falls ~6.5 °C per km of altitude, much as it falls with latitude. The same thermal thresholds therefore produce the same plant zones. Altitude mimics latitude because both are proxies for the same driver.

questions.concept: Why Nepal has so many vegetation types
questions.question: A country only ~200 km wide contains tropical sal forest, temperate oak and alpine meadow. What makes this possible?
questions.solution: Nepal spans an extraordinary ALTITUDINAL range — from ~60 m in the Terai to 8848 m in a short horizontal distance — so the full tropical-to-alpine thermal gradient is compressed into a narrow strip. Combined with monsoon rainfall variation and the rain-shadow north of the Himalaya, almost every Himalayan vegetation type occurs. Diversity comes from steep relief, not from area.

questions.question: Bare rock can eventually support a forest. How do early colonisers make that possible?
questions.solution: Pioneer lichens and mosses secrete organic acids that weather rock and trap particles, slowly building a soil layer; their decomposition adds organic matter and nutrients. As soil depth and water-holding capacity grow, larger plants with bigger root systems can establish, further hastening soil formation. Succession is largely soil-building — the community engineers the conditions for its successor.
